_about: Guided study content. Teaching text is editorial - it is this app's own words and is never Scripture. Not one word of Scripture lives in this file: lessons name references, and scripture:build resolves them against the same pinned WEB corpus the daily readings come from, then emits canonical ids. A reference here that the corpus cannot resolve fails the build.

rules: Ground every explanation in the passage and the context actually read, and list that context in 'basis'.
Explain what the passage says and what a reader needs to know to follow it. Do not add promises, history or doctrine the passage does not carry.
Where a reading is genuinely disputed, state it conservatively or keep it off the centre of the lesson.
Never tell a reader that God selected this lesson for them.
Teach something. Avoiding all interpretation produces a lesson that is safe and useless.

studies.title: New to the Bible
studies.summary: What this collection actually is, the story it tells, and where to begin reading.
studies.audience: Someone opening it for the first time, or coming back after a long gap.

lessons.title: What kind of book this is
lessons.understand:
The Bible is not one book. It is a collection of writings from different times and in different forms — histories, letters, poems, songs, legal codes — brought together as Scripture.

Luke's opening shows what that means in practice. He is a named author writing to a named reader. He says others have already written accounts, that he looked into things himself, and that he is setting them down in order for a stated reason: so that Theophilus can know how reliable the things he was taught really are.

That is a useful expectation to begin with. You are not opening a single argument. You are opening a library, and each piece has an author, an audience and a purpose. Knowing which kind of writing you are in front of changes how you read it.
lessons.lookCloser: Luke says he wrote so his reader could know the certainty of what he had been taught. What does that suggest about the kind of confidence he expected reading to produce?
lessons.reflect: What made you want to open the Bible? Write it down before you begin — it is worth having later.

lessons.title: The story it tells
lessons.understand:
These two passages are separated by the whole of the Bible — the first line of the first book, and a few paragraphs from the end of the last.

Read together they show that the collection has a shape. It opens with God making a world. It closes with God living among people in a world made new, with grief and death gone. Everything in between sits somewhere on that line: what went wrong, what was promised, and what was done about it.

This matters for a beginner because the Bible is easy to read as disconnected fragments — a rule here, a story there, a verse on a card. The individual parts are far easier to place once you know the collection is going somewhere, and where.
lessons.lookCloser: One passage describes a beginning and the other an ending. What is present in both?
lessons.reflect: Which end of that story is easier for you to believe today — the beginning, or the end?

lessons.title: Who Jesus is
lessons.understand:
John opens his account of Jesus by echoing the first words of Genesis — "In the beginning". He is placing Jesus before the creation rather than inside it.

"The Word" translates a Greek term his first readers would have met in discussions of the reason or order behind the world. John takes that familiar idea and does something unexpected with it: the Word is not a principle but someone — who was with God, who was God, and through whom everything was made.

Then verse 14 makes the claim the rest of the book rests on: the one John has been describing did not remain outside the world he made, but took on a human life within it. John is not describing a teacher whose reputation grew after his death. He is claiming that God's own self-expression arrived in a body, and that people saw it.
lessons.lookCloser: Why do you think John chose to open with Jesus as "the Word", rather than with his birth or his teaching?
lessons.reflect: Before today, who did you understand Jesus to be?

lessons.title: What the good news says
lessons.understand:
"Gospel" is an old word meaning good news, and the first passage is the New Testament's own earliest summary of it. Paul says he is handing on something he himself received, which means these lines were already in circulation before he wrote them down.

The summary is short and factual: Christ died for our sins, he was buried, he was raised, and he was seen. Paul then lists people who saw him, several by name, and notes that most of them were still alive — an odd detail to include unless he expected readers to be able to ask them.

The second passage says what this news asks of you, and what it does not. It is described as a gift received rather than a wage earned. The reason given is not that effort is worthless, but that a gift leaves nobody with grounds to boast.
lessons.lookCloser: Paul names witnesses and points out that most were still living. What kind of claim is he making by adding that detail?
lessons.reflect: Which is harder to accept — that the news is true, or that it is free?

lessons.title: How to begin reading
lessons.understand:
Luke describes a group in Beroea who heard Paul preach and then went and checked. They are called more noble for it — not for agreeing quickly, but for receiving eagerly and examining daily to see whether it was so. Testing what you are told is treated here as a credit, not a failure of faith.

The psalm supplies the other half. A lamp at your feet lights the next step, not the whole road. That is a realistic picture of what reading Scripture usually feels like: enough to move by, rarely enough to see the entire route at once.

So begin somewhere concrete rather than at page one. A Gospel is the usual advice, and Luke — whose opening you read in the first lesson — is a reasonable place to start. Read a section rather than a single line.
lessons.lookCloser: The Beroeans examined daily rather than once. What would change if you treated reading as something returned to rather than finished?
lessons.reflect: What is one question you want to keep asking as you read?

studies.title: Who is Jesus?
studies.summary: Who the Gospels say Jesus is, from the promise that came before him to the call he makes on anyone who follows.
studies.audience: Anyone who wants to know what Christians actually claim about Jesus, whether or not they believe it.

lessons.title: The one who was expected
lessons.understand:
Jesus does not arrive in the Gospels as a surprise. He arrives into a people who had been waiting a long time, and the shape of that waiting explains a great deal about what followed.

Isaiah wrote to a nation living under threat, and the promise he gives them is oddly domestic. It is a child. But the titles pile up past anything a child could carry, and the throne named is David’s — the royal line God had promised would not run out.

Centuries later, Luke describes an angel telling a young woman in an unremarkable town that her son will be given that same throne, and that his reign will have no end.

Whatever else the Gospels are doing, they are placing Jesus inside a promise that was already old. The first Christians did not claim he had founded a new religion. They claimed he was what an old one had been waiting for.
lessons.lookCloser: Both passages describe a reign that does not end. What else do the two have in common?
lessons.reflect: Does it change anything to meet Jesus as the answer to a long wait rather than as a new idea?

lessons.title: God’s own likeness, in a human life
lessons.understand:
The letter to the Hebrews opens by comparing two kinds of speech. God had spoken before — through prophets, in pieces, across centuries. Then, the writer says, he spoke again, and this time the message was a person.

That is a larger claim than it sounds. A prophet carries words on God’s behalf. A son is not a delivery method; he carries the family likeness. Hebrews presses exactly there: to look at the Son is to see what God is like, not approximately but exactly.

Two details are easy to read past. The Son is described as holding creation together, so this is not a figure who enters the story late. And after dealing with sin, he sits down. Priests stood at their work, because the work was never finished. Sitting is the posture of someone whose task is complete.
lessons.lookCloser: The passage lists several things the Son does. Which happen before a human life, and which after?
lessons.reflect: If Jesus is meant to show what God is like, how does that compare with the picture you already carry?

lessons.title: The announcement he came making
lessons.understand:
Mark compresses Jesus’ message into one sentence, and what is missing from it matters. There is no instruction, no doctrine, no programme. There is news — that the waiting is over and God’s reign has arrived — and then an invitation to turn around and trust it.

The word kingdom misleads a modern reader, who hears a place. It is closer to a rule actively arriving: what things look like where God is genuinely in charge.

Luke shows the same claim made in a specific room. Jesus reads aloud from Isaiah about someone anointed to bring good news to the poor and freedom to prisoners, hands the scroll back, sits down, and says it has happened today.

Read Isaiah’s sentence to its end and it carries on into judgement. Jesus stops before that clause. What he announces first is release.
lessons.lookCloser: Make a list of what Jesus says he was sent to do. Who are the people named in it?
lessons.reflect: What changes if this is treated as news rather than as advice?

lessons.title: Power that stops for one person
lessons.understand:
Two kinds of power sit side by side here, and the pairing is the lesson.

The first scene is small. A man whose skin disease has cut him off from ordinary human contact does not ask whether Jesus is able to heal him. He asks whether Jesus is willing. Jesus answers first by touching him, which under the law of the time was the one thing nobody did, and then by saying that he is.

The second scene is enormous. A storm that frightens experienced fishermen stops because he tells it to. And the men who have just been rescued end up more afraid afterwards than they were during it.

Their question closes the scene, and it is the question this study is named for. Mark does not answer it. He lets the two scenes stand together: whatever this authority is, it is the kind that stops for one desperate man.
lessons.lookCloser: The man asks about willingness rather than ability. How does the reply answer both?
lessons.reflect: Which is harder to believe — that Jesus could help, or that he would want to?

lessons.title: Why he died
lessons.understand:
Jesus explains his own death before it happens, and he does it in the middle of an argument about rank. His followers want position. He tells them greatness runs the other way, then offers himself as the example — not a leader who serves, but one whose life is handed over for other people.

The word translated ransom carries the sense of a price paid to release someone. Christians have explained how that works in more than one way, and the New Testament uses several images for it. The claim in the passage is narrower and firmer: his death does something for others. It is not merely something done to him.

Isaiah’s poem, far older, describes a figure who suffers in the place of others. The earliest Christians read it as a description of Jesus. In Acts, a man reading this poem asks whether the prophet means himself or someone else, and is told about Jesus.
lessons.lookCloser: Isaiah’s lines move between “he” and “we”. Trace which words belong to which.
lessons.reflect: What difference does it make whether his death was a defeat or something he intended?

lessons.title: The claim that he was raised
lessons.understand:
Luke tells this scene like a man expecting to be doubted.

The disciples’ first thought is that they are seeing a ghost, and Luke says so plainly. He does not present them as people primed to believe. He presents them as frightened, unconvinced, and — in one memorable phrase — unable to accept the news because it is too good.

The evidence he then offers is stubbornly physical. Hands and feet. An invitation to touch. Bones, which a spirit does not have. Finally a piece of cooked fish, eaten in front of them.

Whatever a reader concludes about it, it is worth being clear what is being claimed. Not that Jesus survived. Not that his memory endured, or that his friends went on feeling his presence. The claim is that an executed man was alive again, in a body, and hungry.
lessons.lookCloser: Count the ways Luke shows this is a body rather than a vision.
lessons.reflect: The first witnesses doubted. Does it help or hinder you that their doubt was written down?

lessons.title: What following him costs
lessons.understand:
The setting matters. Moments earlier Peter has said out loud that Jesus is the Messiah, and Jesus has answered by describing his own rejection and death. Only then does he turn to the crowd and say what following him will involve.

Carrying a cross has softened into a phrase for putting up with hardship. It did not mean that. A cross was an execution, and the people listening had seen them used. He is describing a life no longer arranged around self-protection.

Then he states the exchange, and it lands as an observation rather than a threat: gripping your life is precisely how you lose it. What he offers is not a better life in the ordinary sense. It is a different kind of one, and he says the price out loud before anyone agrees to it.

That refusal to undersell is itself part of the answer to who he is.
lessons.lookCloser: The words life and save each appear more than once, and not always meaning the same thing. Which is which?
lessons.reflect: What would it look like to arrange a life around something other than protecting it?

studies.title: Understanding the Gospel
studies.summary: What Christians mean by the word gospel, followed through Scripture from a good creation to a life remade.
studies.audience: Anyone who has heard the word for years without having it explained, or had it explained too fast.

lessons.title: A world made on purpose
lessons.understand:
Most short accounts of the Christian message open with what has gone wrong. Genesis opens earlier, and the order matters: before there is anything to rescue, there is something worth rescuing.

Two claims sit in these lines. The first is that people are made in God’s image. The text never explains what that likeness consists of, and Christians have discussed it for centuries — but it does something more immediate. It assigns a standing. Dignity here is not achieved and not handed out by merit. It is given, and given to everyone in view, without qualification.

The second is the verdict at the end of the day’s work. Not adequate. Not acceptable. Very good.

Hold both, because everything that follows depends on them. What comes next in this story is a tear in something that was good to start with, which is why it reads as loss rather than as the way things always were.
lessons.lookCloser: Who is included in what is said about God’s image, and who is left out?
lessons.reflect: If human dignity is given rather than earned, what would follow from taking that seriously?

lessons.title: The hiding
lessons.understand:
Notice what comes first. Not a thunderbolt. A couple hiding among the trees, and a God who comes looking and asks where they are.

That is this book’s picture of what has gone wrong, and it is more relational than legal. The damage surfaces as fear, concealment, and a new distance between people and the God who made them. Sin here is not primarily a list of infractions. It is a relationship broken from one side.

Paul, writing far later, refuses to let anyone stand outside the problem. Everyone falls short. The aim is not to induce shame; it is to remove the ranking, because there is no group in the room that does not need help.

And he does not stop at the diagnosis. The same sentence runs on into a gift. Christians often use the word justified for this — being put right with God freely, because of Christ, rather than because the account was eventually balanced.
lessons.lookCloser: God asks a question. What does the man’s answer reveal about what has changed between them?
lessons.reflect: What do people tend to do with the parts of themselves they would rather not have seen?

lessons.title: God’s move toward us
lessons.understand:
Between the hiding in Genesis and the arrival of Jesus lies most of the Bible, and it is tempting to read those centuries as a delay. They read better as the rescue already under way.

God’s answer to a broken world is neither to abandon it nor to repair it on the spot. He calls one man out of one country and makes him a short list of promises. Land. Descendants. A name.

But the promise does not stop with Abram, and the last line is the one to watch. The blessing is aimed outward, at every family on earth. Whatever else this nation’s story becomes, it begins with a stated intention to reach past itself.

Paul later points at this exact sentence and calls it the good news announced ahead of time. On that reading, what happens in Jesus is not a change of plan. It is an old promise being kept.
lessons.lookCloser: Count the promises made to Abram. Which of them rest on him, and which on God?
lessons.reflect: What is the difference between a God who fixes the world instantly and one who works through a long history?

lessons.title: The cross, and who it was for
lessons.understand:
Paul is arguing about timing, and the weight of it rests on a single word: while.

He sets the comparison up carefully. People do occasionally die for someone worth dying for; a genuinely good person might inspire it. That, he says, is roughly the outer limit of ordinary human love — and even there, the one being died for has to be worth it.

Then he puts the cross outside that limit. Christ died for people who were not worth it and had not asked. Not once they improved. Not after they had made themselves presentable. While.

How the cross achieves what it achieves has been discussed for as long as there have been Christians, and the New Testament reaches for several images. Paul’s concern in these three verses is narrower. He is using the timing to show what kind of love this is: love that moves first, toward people who have given it no reason to.
lessons.lookCloser: Paul describes the people Christ died for three times, using three different words. What are they?
lessons.reflect: What changes if love arrived before there was anything in you to reward?

lessons.title: Why the resurrection is not optional
lessons.understand:
It would be easy to treat the resurrection as a happy ending fastened onto the important part. Paul refuses that arrangement, and he does it by saying out loud what follows if it never happened.

Read what he is prepared to concede. If Christ was not raised, faith is empty, forgiveness has not occurred, the Christian dead are simply dead, and believers are the most pitiable people alive. He reaches for no fallback — not that the teaching is still wise, not that the community is still worthwhile. He lets the whole thing stand or fall on an event.

Then comes the turn, and one phrase carries it. First fruit is a harvest word. The first sheaf is not the point of a harvest; it is the evidence that the rest of the field is coming.

So the claim is not only that one man was raised. It is that his rising has opened something meant to include others.
lessons.lookCloser: Paul lists what would be true if Christ were not raised. How many separate consequences does he name?
lessons.reflect: Paul stakes everything on an event rather than on the value of the teaching. Why might that matter?

lessons.title: Grace, and the life that follows
lessons.understand:
Two words hold this passage together, and their order is the entire point.

The first is gift. Paul’s language is pointedly financial in what it rules out: not wages, not achievement, nothing anyone could invoice for. He presses further than most summaries dare — the people being rescued are called dead, and death is not a condition that contributes to its own recovery.

The second is workmanship. Having ruled out earning, Paul does not conclude that behaviour has stopped mattering. He says the reverse. Good works are not the price of the rescue; they are what the rescued life is for, and he pictures them as already prepared, waiting to be walked into.

This is where the shortest summaries of the Christian message usually fail. What is described here is not an arrangement for securing a destination. It is a person made alive now, for a life with a shape to it.
lessons.lookCloser: Find the two things Paul says this rescue does not come by, and the one thing he says it is for.
lessons.reflect: If good works follow the gift rather than pay for it, what does that change about trying to live well?

studies.title: Learning to Pray
studies.summary: What prayer is in Scripture, how Jesus taught it, and how to begin — including what to do when nothing seems to come back.
studies.audience: Anyone who wants to pray and is unsure how to start, or who started once and stopped.

lessons.title: What prayer actually is
lessons.understand:
Jesus starts by clearing away two mistakes, and both are still with us.

The first is prayer as performance. He describes people praying where they are certain to be seen, and observes — dryly — that they have already got what they came for. His remedy is almost comically plain: shut the door.

The second is prayer as word-count, as though God responded to volume the way a reluctant official responds to persistence. His reason for dismissing that is the surprising part: your Father already knows what you need.

Which could sound like an argument for not bothering. It is the opposite. If prayer is not how God gets informed, then it was never a transaction, and the anxiety about phrasing it correctly falls away. The psalm supplies the picture: pour it out. Not compose it. Not perform it. Pour.
lessons.lookCloser: Jesus names two habits to avoid and gives a reason for each. What are the two reasons?
lessons.reflect: Which of these two mistakes is closer to your own instinct about prayer?

lessons.title: The prayer he gave them
lessons.understand:
Asked for a model, Jesus gives one short enough to memorise, and its shape teaches as much as its wording.

Look at the order. Three lines about God come before anything about the person praying — his name, his reign, his will. Whatever else this is, it is not a form for submitting requests. It begins by getting the room the right way round.

Then the asking, and it is modest. Bread for today, not security for the year. Forgiveness, with a clause attached that ought to slow anyone down, since it ties the receiving to the giving. Protection from testing and from evil.

One detail is easy to miss. Every request is plural. Our bread, our debts, deliver us. Even prayed alone in a shut room, this is not a private arrangement.
lessons.lookCloser: Three requests concern God and three concern the people praying. Where exactly does it turn?
lessons.reflect: The prayer puts God’s concerns before its own. What would it take to pray in that order?

lessons.title: Honest prayer
lessons.understand:
Four times in two verses, the same question: how long. The psalm accuses God of forgetting and of hiding his face. It is not polite, and nobody edited it out. It sits in the collection Israel actually used for worship.

That placement is worth pausing over. If this is in the prayer book, then complaint is not a failure of prayer. It is a form of prayer, and a permitted one. Whatever honesty before God costs, it does not cost admission.

Then the psalm turns, and how it turns matters. The writer says he trusts, that his heart is glad, that he will sing. Read those closing lines again and notice what is absent. Nothing says the enemy left. Nothing reports that the situation resolved.

The turn is not relief arriving. It is a decision made while still waiting, which is a far more usable model than the alternative.
lessons.lookCloser: The psalm changes direction near the end. What has changed by that point, and what has not?
lessons.reflect: What would change if prayer had room for the kind of bluntness this psalm uses?

lessons.title: Asking, and the answer that was no
lessons.understand:
This is the passage to keep when prayer appears not to work.

In the garden, Jesus asks to be spared what is coming. He does not phrase it cautiously; he says plainly that God is able to do it. And the answer is no.

That fact deserves its full weight. If prayer were a dependable mechanism for obtaining outcomes, this prayer would have worked. Whatever unanswered prayer means, it cannot mean the one praying lacked faith or asked badly.

Notice the order, too. He asks for what he genuinely wants, fully, and only then yields. Surrender does not replace the request; it follows it. A prayer that starts out already resigned has skipped a step he did not skip.

Paul writes about anxiety and prayer, and it repays reading precisely. What he promises is not the outcome requested. It is peace — described as something that guards a person, which is language for what holds when circumstances do not.
lessons.lookCloser: Jesus states what God is able to do and what he himself wants. How does his last sentence hold both?
lessons.reflect: How does it sit with you that Jesus asked for something and did not receive it?

lessons.title: Prayer in an ordinary week
lessons.understand:
Luke gives one sentence to Jesus’ prayer habit, and its placement does the work. The crowds are growing. The demand is rising. That is the moment Luke chooses to mention he kept going off alone to pray.

Not that he found time. That he withdrew — deliberately, and repeatedly. Prayer here is not what is left over at the end of a day; it is defended against the day.

Paul’s instruction sounds impossible until you notice what it cannot mean. Nobody speaks continuously. What he describes is closer to a line kept open — a running relationship rather than a scheduled event, where thanks and requests surface as the hours go.

Together they suggest something practical. Set aside a time small enough that you will genuinely keep it, and let the rest of the day stay open. The aim was never eloquence. It was contact, sustained.
lessons.lookCloser: Luke reports what the crowds were doing and what Jesus did. How are the two connected?
lessons.reflect: What would a small, sustainable prayer habit look like in your actual week?
